subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage: "Jaya, when I was an engineer, our team built a small bridge model for a big competition. Our leader was loud and clever. But the best idea, to use triangles for strength, came from Sunil, the quietest boy. When we won, our leader took the stage and said, 'My idea.' Sunil just looked at his shoes. I felt sick. So I stood up and said, 'Actually, Sunil thought of the triangles.' People clapped for him. Since then, whenever I lead, I name who did what." Kalyani Aaji tapped Jaya's group chart. "So who had your best idea?"

qa.q: What idea did Sunil have?
qa.a: He suggested using triangles for strength.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani feel sick when the leader took credit?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair and could see how hurt Sunil was.

qa.q: What lesson does Kalyani give Jaya about group work?
qa.a: She tells Jaya to name who did what and give credit fairly.

qa.q: How might Sunil have felt when Kalyani spoke up?
qa.a: He likely felt surprised and grateful to be recognised.

grounding: An elder tells a story about roles in a group and giving credit fairly.

subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage: The science model was due tomorrow, and the rain had soaked their cardboard on the balcony. Kamal and Payal had one evening to start again, and no money for new craft paper. "You cut, I'll glue," Kamal said. Payal stared at the kitchen shelf, then had an idea. "Let's use old bottle caps for the wheels." They worked until the cart rolled across the floor. At school the next day, the teacher spun a wheel and praised Kamal. "Great wheels!" Kamal said, "That was Payal's idea. I just glued." Payal smiled shyly.

qa.q: What did Payal suggest for the wheels?
qa.a: Payal suggested using old bottle caps.

qa.q: Why did Payal smile shyly?
qa.a: Payal felt happy and a little embarrassed that Kamal gave Payal the credit.

qa.q: Which of Kamal's choices made the teamwork fair?
qa.a: Kamal divided roles and gave Payal credit for the idea.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Kamal after giving credit?
qa.a: The teacher might respect Kamal's fairness and honesty.

grounding: It shows children dividing roles and sharing credit fairly under time pressure.

subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage: In their Hyderabad classroom, Alka's group of four was making a poster on water saving. Alka organised who would write the slogans, who would colour and who would find facts in the library book. Chetan, the quietest, hardly spoke, but he drew a beautiful dripping tap in the middle, each drop shaded blue. When the poster went up, the teacher said, "Wonderful poster, Alka!" Alka pointed. "Chetan drew the tap. The other two found the facts. I just planned it." Chetan's ears went pink. Later he offered to help her with the next poster.

qa.q: What did Chetan draw in the middle of the poster?
qa.a: He drew a beautiful dripping tap.

qa.q: What does Chetan's pink ears suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt embarrassed but pleased to be noticed.

qa.q: What did Alka do as a leader that helped the group?
qa.a: She organised roles and shared the credit fairly.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel about working with Alka again?
qa.a: He seems keen, as he offered to help with the next poster.

grounding: It shows a child acting as leader and giving credit fairly in a group task.

subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage: 'So who's presenting the volcano model tomorrow?' Jaya asked, stirring the dal. 'Me,' said Uma. 'I'm group leader.' 'And the others?' 'Tariq painted the lava. Sunny found the baking soda trick in the library book. And Mili just cut paper.' 'Just?' Uma licked a spoon. 'Well, she cut all the paper trees. Forty-two.' 'Forty-two trees! And when Ma'am asks who did what?' Uma was quiet. 'I was going to say I made it.' 'Did you?' 'I organised it. That's different, isn't it?' Jaya smiled. 'Very.' Uma sat up. 'I'll say everyone's part. Even the trees. Mili never talks in class. She'll like that.' 'Leaders do that.'

qa.q: How many paper trees did Mili cut?
qa.a: Mili cut forty-two paper trees.

qa.q: What does Uma's quiet moment suggest she was realising?
qa.a: She was realising that claiming she made the model would be unfair, since each person contributed a different part.

qa.q: What could Uma say in class tomorrow to share credit fairly?
qa.a: She could name each member's part: Tariq's lava, Sunny's baking soda trick, Mili's trees and her own organising.

qa.q: How might Mili feel hearing her trees mentioned in class?
qa.a: She would likely feel noticed and proud, especially since she rarely speaks up herself. 😊

grounding: Shows a child in a leader role recognising others' roles and choosing to give credit fairly.

subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage: At our school science fair last year, Gurpreet and I built a burglar alarm with a buzzer. I painted the cardboard house and wrote the chart. Gurpreet did the wiring, which was the hard part; he burnt his thumb once on the soldering iron. On the day, the judge came to our table and looked at me because I was standing in front. 'Did you design this circuit?' she asked. For one second I wanted to just say yes. She was smiling at me. Then I saw Gurpreet looking at his shoes. 'No, ma'am, he did. I did the house and chart.' She turned to him with questions. We won second prize. I'm Madhuri; I still remember his grin.

qa.q: What part of the project did Gurpreet do?
qa.a: Gurpreet did the wiring for the burglar alarm.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri, for one second, want to say yes to the judge?
qa.a: The judge was smiling at her, and taking the praise felt tempting in that moment.

qa.q: What went right when Madhuri answered the judge?
qa.a: She named Gurpreet's real work and her own smaller part, so the judge questioned the right person.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have felt while looking at his shoes?
qa.a: He may have felt overlooked and unsure whether his work would be noticed, then relieved when Madhuri spoke up.

grounding: A child in a contributor role gives fair credit to a teammate for his work.
